opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things that make it really hard. One is that, unlike language or images, we don't have an internet's worth of robot data lying around. If you want a model to learn how to fold laundry or wipe down a counter, someone has to actually collect that data on a physical robot, and that's slow and expensive. So we're starting from a much smaller pool than people working on language models had.

The second is that the physical world is just incredibly diverse and unforgiving. Every kitchen is different, every object has slightly different weight and friction and deformability, the lighting changes, things get moved around. A robot that works beautifully in one lab can fall apart when you put it in someone's home. Getting that kind of generalization, where a robot can handle a scene or an object it's never seen before, is really the core challenge.

And then there's the fact that it's a closed-loop problem. The robot isn't just producing an output that a person reads. It's taking actions that change the world, and then it has to react to the consequences of those actions in real time. Small errors compound. If you grasp something a little bit off, the next step is now harder, and if you haven't seen data on how to recover from that mistake, things can go off the rails quickly.

On top of that you have hardware: robots break, they're costly, they're not standardized, so it's hard to pool data across different platforms. Put all of that together and it's a much tougher problem than it might look from the outside. But I'm actually pretty optimistic, because I think a lot of the lessons from scaling in other areas of machine learning, like training large models on diverse data, are starting to transfer to robotics, and we're seeing real progress on generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first is that the physical world is just really messy and really diverse. If you think about something like language, there's a lot of structure there, and we have this enormous amount of data on the internet that captures a lot of what people care about. In robotics, the robot has to deal with lighting changes, with objects that deform, with clutter, with a drawer that sticks a little bit differently than the last one it opened. Every one of those variations is something the robot has to handle, and the long tail of those situations is enormous.

The second thing is data. For language models, the data already existed. People wrote text for decades, and it was sitting there waiting to be used. For robots, there is no equivalent. There's no internet of robot experience. So if you want a robot to learn how to fold laundry or cook a meal, you either have to collect that data yourself, which is slow and expensive, or you have to find clever ways to get it from somewhere else, like simulation or human videos, and those come with their own gaps.

And then the third piece is that robotics is a closed loop problem. When a language model makes a mistake, you can just regenerate or edit the output. When a robot makes a mistake, it's now in a state it has never seen before, and it has to recover from that. Errors compound over time. So the bar for reliability is much higher, and small mistakes can actually matter a lot, especially when there's a physical object or a person involved.

I'd also add that you can't just throw compute at it in the same way. You're limited by real time, by hardware that breaks, by the fact that you can only run so many robots at once. So the iteration loop is just fundamentally slower than it is in a lot of other areas of machine learning. That said, I'm actually pretty optimistic. A lot of the tools we've developed for language and vision do transfer, and we're starting to see what happens when you combine those with even modest amounts of robot data. It's starting to feel like the ingredients are coming together.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is hard because you have to get a lot of things right at the same time. You need to perceive the world, figure out what to do, and then actually execute that action. And those pieces are tightly coupled. If your perception is a little bit off, you might miss the object you’re trying to grasp, and now you need to recognize that and recover.

The physical world is also really varied. Something as simple as picking up a cup depends on its shape, what it’s made of, whether it’s full, and what’s around it. Humans handle those differences almost without thinking, but getting a robot to generalize across them is challenging.

And then there’s the data problem. For language, there’s this enormous amount of text on the internet that you can learn from. There isn’t an equivalent supply of robot experience. You have to collect it by having robots interact with the world, which takes time, and things break. So you’re trying to learn a very broad set of capabilities with data that’s much harder to obtain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is hard because it brings together a lot of problems that are difficult on their own. You need to perceive the world, understand what matters for a task, and then choose actions that change the world in the way you want. And all of that has to work in the physical world, where things are messy and uncertain. An object might slip, the lighting might change, or something might be in a slightly different place than you expected.

One of the biggest challenges is data. If you’re training a language model, there’s an enormous amount of text on the internet. There isn’t an equivalent internet of robot interactions. A video can show you what someone did, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you the forces they applied or what would have happened if they’d moved differently. So robots need to collect experience, and collecting that experience is relatively slow.

And then there’s generalization. You don’t want a robot that can pick up one particular cup in one particular kitchen. You want it to handle a cup it’s never seen, in a home it’s never been in, and recover when something goes wrong. Getting that kind of flexibility and reliability together is really challenging.
